title: Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 December)
hook: the patroness of the Americas; roses in December

segments.voice: Yesterday, kecharitomene: not the virgin birth, but Mary herself, full of grace from the start. Did anyone mix them up around you? Day six hundred thirty-six.

Before dawn on December 12, in Mexico City and in parishes from Los Angeles to Chicago, people gather outside churches to sing Las Mañanitas, the birthday song, to Mary. Mariachis in the dark. Roses everywhere, in buckets, in arms, in front of a framed image of a young woman with her head bowed, dressed in a starred mantle, standing on a crescent moon. Her basilica in Mexico City stands at the foot of a hill. The story behind all those roses begins with a poor man on that hill in winter.
screen: `SINGING IN THE DARK.` → `ROSES EVERYWHERE.` → `A MAN ON A HILL.`

segments.voice: December 1531, in the years just after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec capital. Juan Diego, an Indigenous man and a recent convert, is walking past the hill of Tepeyac. He hears birdsong, then a voice calling him by name. A young woman, speaking his own language, Nahuatl, tells him she is the Mother of the true God and asks for a church to be built there. He goes to the bishop, Juan de Zumárraga, who is unconvinced and asks for a sign. Then Juan Diego's uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, embarrassed, takes a different path around the hill to fetch a priest and avoid her. She meets him anyway. The best-known account gives her words, in paraphrase: do not be afraid; am I not here, I who am your mother? She tells him his uncle is already healed and sends him up the hill, where in the cold of December he finds roses blooming. He gathers them into his tilma, his rough cloak, and carries them to the bishop. When he opens it, the roses fall, and on the cloth is the image people still visit today. The fullest account, the Nican Mopohua, was published in Nahuatl in 1649, and historians debate how early the story was written down; the Church's devotion rests on long tradition and on the image itself. In 2002, Pope John Paul II canonized Juan Diego. Popes have named Mary under this title patroness of the Americas. In the story, notice who she chooses: not the bishop, but a conquered man, addressed in his own tongue, by name.
screen: `TEPEYAC, DECEMBER 1531.` · `THE BISHOP ASKS FOR A SIGN.` · `AM I NOT HERE?` · `ROSES IN THE TILMA.` · then, large: `I WHO AM YOUR MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring a flower to a church, or plan to. If there's a church near you, picture the walk, the door, the place by an image of Mary where people leave roses. If you can go today, take one flower. For now, sit and think of someone who has said to you, in their own way, I'm here. A parent, a friend, a stranger in a hard hour. If you pray, you can offer that person and that flower to Our Lady. If you don't, simply give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Nican Mopohua, 'here it is told.' The Nahuatl account of Mary's appearance to Juan Diego at Tepeyac in 1531, published in 1649. Today's word.
Your line: am I not here. Today, be the one who shows up for someone who's taking the long way around. Day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: On December 12 many Catholics, especially Mexican and Mexican-American communities, gather before dawn to sing Las Mañanitas to Our Lady of Guadalupe and bring roses to her image.

original.note: Nahuatl, written in Latin letters: 'here it is told', the opening words and title of the account.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guadalupe is a Mexican picture of Mary.
what it means: Mary as she appeared, by tradition, to an Indigenous man at Tepeyac in 1531, honored as patroness of the Americas.
what a scholar hears: the Nican Mopohua was published in Nahuatl in 1649; historians debate how early the account was written down.

notes: Words of Our Lady ('am I not here, I who am your mother?') are paraphrased from the Nican Mopohua; no public-domain English translation is quoted.
Patroness of the Americas: Pius XII (1945, 'Empress of the Americas'); John Paul II (1999, Ecclesia in America) for all America. Confirm wording 'popes have named'.
Historiography: the Nican Mopohua published 1649, attributed to Antonio Valeriano; scholars debate earlier documentation. Confirm the neutral phrasing.
Roses identified in tradition as Castilian roses; not stated. Visitor numbers given only as 'millions'.
In the United States, December 12 is a feast; confirm rank for the Keeper's preferred framing.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'millions every year', 'nearly five hundred years' and 'ten years after the conquest'; the bishop is 'unconvinced', not 'polite'.
